title: the rule that keeps turning up
hookLine: the rule that keeps turning up
tomorrow: start with the person in the mirror

lines: TREAT PEOPLE THE WAY YOU WANT TO BE TREATED.
cards: A playground, right after somebody grabbed something that wasn't theirs. A grown-up crouches down and says it: treat people the way you want to be treated. Plenty of kids hear it before they can read.

It's so familiar it sounds like nothing. But here's the strange part. You can find it in ancient China, in Jewish law, in the sayings of the rabbis, in the words of Jesus, in India's great epic, in Greek writers.
It turns up on path after path.

teach.b: Start in China. A student asks Confucius if there's one word you could live by your whole life.
In an old translation, Confucius answers: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Notice it's a don't.
The Hebrew Bible, in among laws about harvests and fair wages, says to love your neighbor as yourself.

teach.h: HILLEL: THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.
teach.b: Centuries later, a man asks the rabbi Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. Hillel says, roughly: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor.
That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn it.

teach.h: JESUS: DO YE EVEN SO TO THEM.
teach.b: Then Jesus puts it as a do: "all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." India's great epic has a version. So does the Greek orator Isocrates.
Did each path arrive at it on its own? Nobody can say for sure who heard what from whom. What's clear is that it keeps turning up, and each tradition keeps it in its own place.
For Confucius it's one word for a whole life. For Hillel, a summary that sends you back to study. For Jesus, the law and the prophets in a sentence.
And notice where the rule starts: with you. What you don't want. What you would want.
It asks you to use your own heart as a map of someone else's.

how: The golden rule is taught in many religious and ethical settings: Jewish teaching often recalls Hillel's saying, Christian teaching the Sermon on the Mount, Confucian teaching the Analects, and families often pass it to children as an early rule.

games.q: who said it — tap the pairs.

s: the golden rule is found only in the Gospels
Leviticus, Hillel, Confucius, the Mahabharata and Isocrates all have versions.
Confucius put it as a don't
"what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others."
Jesus puts the rule as a do
"do ye even so to them." Confucius and Hillel put it as a don't.

games.q: a man asks the rabbi Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. what does Hillel do?
o: sums it up in one line, then says: go and learn.
games.why: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; the rest is commentary; go and learn. in the Talmud's story, another rabbi, Shammai, had already sent the man away.

practice: Here's the practice. From today the bell gives you a little longer, about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle.
Think of someone you'll see today. Then ask: if I were them, today, what would I want? Maybe to be listened to.
Maybe to be left alone for a bit. Maybe just a real hello. Let the answer settle.
You don't have to do anything with it yet. Just know it.

wordCard.voice: The golden rule. What you'd want, given. What you'd hate, held back. Found on path after path. Fifteenth word.

orig.note: Chinese, shu: Confucius's one word for a whole life (Analects 15:23). Legge translates it reciprocity.

carryVoice: Your line: be good to people. Your own heart already knows the map. See you tomorrow.
